seo.shortDescription: Searchable duty table for all 121 HTS Chapter 22 lines — water, soft drinks, beer, wine, sparkling wine, cider, sake, ethanol, whisky, vodka, gin, rum, tequila, brandy, liqueurs and vinegar. General, FTA and Column 2 rates, the 2026 Section 301 duties and the Canada Section 338 alcohol duties and import ban.

overview.intro:
Chapter 22 covers beverages: water and soft drinks, beer, wine, cider and sake, ethyl alcohol, spirits — whisky, vodka, gin, rum, tequila, brandy, liqueurs — and vinegar. Its **121 tariff lines** carry low printed rates: **beer and almost all spirits are Free**, still wine pays **6.3¢ to 22.4¢ per liter** and sparkling wine **19.8¢ per liter**, a fraction of 1% of value for most bottles.

The U.S. imported **$28.00B** of Chapter 22 goods in 2025 — Mexican beer ($6.10B) and tequila and other Mexican spirits ($3.80B), French and Italian wine ($4.61B together) and Scotch and other British spirits ($1.30B). What the importer pays now depends on the extra duties: since **July 24, 2026** goods of 60 economies pay a Section 301 duty — **10% in total for EU wine, beer and spirits**, +10% for the UK (**Scotch and Irish whisky exempt**), 12.5% for Japan, Australia, New Zealand and Chile. USMCA-qualifying Mexican beer and tequila enter free. **Canada** pays 50% under Section 338 since August 22, 2026, and from **September 29, 2026** bottled Canadian wine, whisky and other spirits, and packaged Canadian beer and cider, may not be imported at all.

productGroups.label: Mineral and aerated water, ice and snow (unsweetened)
productGroups.blurb: Mineral and sparkling water pay 0.26¢/liter; other water, ice and snow are Free. Italy ($489M), France ($223M) and Fiji ($189M) are the main suppliers. Bottled water must meet FDA's bottled-water standard.

productGroups.label: Soft drinks, flavored water, energy drinks and other non-alcoholic beverages (incl. non-alcoholic beer)
productGroups.blurb: Soft drinks, energy drinks, non-alcoholic beer and plant-based drinks pay 0.2¢/liter. Milk-based drinks pay 17%–17.5% or, over the dairy quota, 23.5¢/liter + 14.9%; fortified juices follow the juice rates. Mexico ($980M) and Canada ($539M) supply the most.

productGroups.label: Beer made from malt
productGroups.blurb: Beer is Free. It is the largest product in the chapter — $7.21B in 2025, $6.10B of it from Mexico. USMCA-qualifying Mexican beer pays nothing; EU beer pays 10% in total since July 24, 2026. From April 2025 to April 2026 the aluminum in beer cans also paid the Section 232 aluminum duty.

productGroups.label: Wine of fresh grapes (still and sparkling) and grape must
productGroups.blurb: Still wine in bottles pays 6.3¢/liter up to 14% alcohol (16.9¢ for sherry and other strong wine), in bag-in-box or bulk 8.4¢–22.4¢/liter; sparkling wine and Champagne 19.8¢/liter. France ($2.46B), Italy ($2.15B) and New Zealand ($500M) lead. EU wine pays 10% in total since July 24, 2026.

productGroups.label: Vermouth and other flavored wine
productGroups.blurb: Vermouth and other wine flavored with plants pay 3.5¢–4.2¢ per liter; almost all comes from Italy ($127M).

productGroups.label: Cider, perry, mead, sake and other fermented beverages
productGroups.blurb: Hard cider pays 0.4¢/liter, sake 3¢/liter, hard seltzers and other fermented drinks 4.2¢/liter. Canada ($138M), Japan ($89M, mostly sake) and Mexico ($76M) are the main suppliers.

productGroups.label: Ethyl alcohol (undenatured 80%+ and denatured), incl. fuel ethanol
productGroups.blurb: Beverage-grade alcohol pays 18.9¢ per proof liter; fuel and industrial ethanol 2.5% (undenatured) or 1.9% (denatured). Brazil ($151M) and Canada ($103M) supply most.

productGroups.label: Spirits, liqueurs and other spirituous beverages (whisky, vodka, gin, rum, tequila, brandy)
productGroups.blurb: Whisky, vodka, gin, tequila, mezcal, brandy, Cognac and liqueurs are Free; cheap rum (23.7¢/pf. liter) and premixed cocktails (21.1¢/pf. liter) are the exceptions. $8.96B in 2025: Mexico (tequila, $3.80B), France (Cognac, $1.51B), the UK (Scotch, $1.30B) and Canada ($680M). Scotch and Irish whisky from the UK are exempt from the UK Section 301 duty.

productGroups.label: Vinegar
productGroups.blurb: Vinegar pays 0.5¢ per proof liter; Italy ($134M, mostly balsamic) is by far the largest supplier. A new statistical split separates certified-organic vinegar.

rateTable.note: Rates shown in grey are inherited from the parent heading. HTSUS states a duty once on the 8-digit line and leaves the 10-digit statistical lines blank; this table resolves each line to the rate that actually applies to it.

notes.additionalUsNotes:
**Note 1.** Chapter 22 duties are in addition to the internal-revenue (excise) taxes, and are charged only on the quantities subject to those taxes; for spirits transferred to a bonded distilled spirits plant, on the quantity withdrawn from customs custody.

**Note 2.** 2202.99.30–2202.99.37 cover vitamin- or mineral-fortified fruit and vegetable juices imported only in non-concentrated form; concentrated ones go to 2106.90.48, 2106.90.52 or 2106.90.54.

**Note 3.** Dutiable quantities of alcoholic juices (including grape must) in 2204, 2206 or 2208 are calculated under additional U.S. notes 1–3 to chapter 20.

**Note 4.** "Effervescent wine" is wine other than sparkling wine containing more than 0.392 g of carbon dioxide per 100 ml.

**Notes 5–7.** A "proof liter" is a liter at 15.56°C (60°F) containing 50% (100 proof) ethyl alcohol by volume; per-proof-liter rates are scaled to the product's actual proof, which is measured as under the internal-revenue laws.

**Note 8.** Free entry of certain alcoholic beverage samples is provided in 9811.00.20 (chapter 98).

**Note 9.** The standard proof of vinegar (2209) is 4% acetic acid by weight.

**Statistical notes.** "Hard cider" (2206.00.15.10) is an apple or pear fermented beverage with no other fruit or flavoring, more than 0.5% and less than 8.5% alcohol and at most 0.64 g of carbon dioxide per 100 ml; certified-organic splits follow general statistical note 6.

seo.title: HTS Chapter 22 Beverage & Alcohol Tariff Updates — Canada Ban, Section 301, Wine & Spirits Since 2025 | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: What changed for beverage and alcohol imports (HTS Chapter 22) since January 2025: the Canada Section 338 duties and import ban, the 2026 Section 301 tariffs on EU wine and spirits, the Scotch exemption, the aluminum duty on canned beer, and the end of the IEEPA and Section 122 duties, with Federal Register citations.

tariffUpdates.intro:
This page compares two editions of the tariff schedule: the **2025 Basic Edition**, in force at the start of 2025, and the current **2026 Revision 21** (in force October 9, 2026). **No Chapter 22 base rate changed**: 112 of the 121 lines are identical and the other 9 are new statistical splits — certified-organic vodka, tequila and vinegar, and almond-based drinks — at the parent's rate.

The changes came on top. The 2025 IEEPA duties ended on **February 24, 2026**, and the 10% Section 122 surcharge that replaced them expired on July 23, 2026. Canned beer paid the Section 232 duty on its aluminum from April 4, 2025 until April 6, 2026. Since **July 24, 2026** goods of 60 economies pay a Section 301 duty — **10% in total for EU wine, beer and spirits**, +10% for the UK with **Scotch and Irish whisky exempt**, 12.5% for Japan, Australia, New Zealand and Chile. **Canada** pays 50% under Section 338 since August 22, 2026, and from **September 29, 2026** most Canadian wine and spirits, and packaged Canadian beer and cider, are banned.
tariffUpdates.scope: Measures that reach Chapter 22 from any country: the 2026 Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies with the UK whisky exception, the Brazil Section 301 tariff, the older China Section 301 lists, the Canada Section 338 duties and import bans, the Section 232 aluminum duty on canned beer (ended April 6, 2026, except for Russia), the Nicaragua Section 301 tariff that starts in 2027, and the 2025–2026 IEEPA and Section 122 duties that have ended. For the rate each supplier pays, see Rates by country.

understandIndustry.why:
U.S. imports of Chapter 22 goods fell from **$32.60B in 2024 to $28.00B in 2025** (−14.1%), the lowest since 2020 ($26.89B). The drop is mostly **spirits**: heading 2208 fell from $12.10B to $8.96B (−26%) — "other" spirits, mostly tequila, from $5.66B to $3.90B, Cognac and grape brandy −33% to $875M, vodka −25%, whisky −21% to $1.49B. Beer slipped 6.9% to $7.21B and wine 8% to $6.54B.

By supplier, Mexico fell 15.4% to $11.12B, France 15.4% to $4.31B, Italy 7.5% to $3.34B and the UK 27.1% to $1.46B. Most Mexican beer and tequila entered duty-free under USMCA throughout 2025, so their decline was not driven by tariffs; for EU and UK goods the 10% reciprocal duty from April 5, 2025 (15% in total for the EU from August 7) added to the cost, and canned beer from every country paid the aluminum duty on its cans from April 4, 2025.

Canada ($1.56B, −3.3%) was little changed in 2025; the 50% Section 338 duty (August 22, 2026) and the import ban (September 29, 2026) came after the latest full year of data, as did the 2026 Section 301 duties.

The total rate on beverages depends mostly on **where they come from**, because the base rates are small or Free. assumptions: Each total was computed by the official-measures calculator engine (the same data as the tariff calculator: measures.json, HTSUS 2026 Revision 21) for goods entered on 2026-10-12, priced on a $10,000 shipment and 1,000 units for per-unit rates.
Ranges like "Free · 11.8%" mean the group has lines with different base rates; select a cell to see which lines carry which rate.
A per-unit rate plus a percentage cannot be added into one number without the shipment’s weight, count or volume, so it is shown as written.

Preferences: USMCA (S) is applied for Canada and Mexico on the "USMCA-qualifying" side; AU for Australia and CL for Chile. GSP (A, A+) has been expired since December 31, 2020 and is not applied. An FTA claim removes the base rate but not the Section 301 duty (U.S. note 52(a)), and for Canada it does not remove the Section 338 duty (U.S. note 51(a)).
Any other country shows the range across every country not listed (column 2 countries — Cuba, North Korea, Russia, Belarus — aside), without preferences.

Fortified juices of 2202.99.36 and 2202.99.37 take "the rate applicable to the natural juice in heading 2009" (Chapter 20), which depends on the juice; their totals are shown as that rate plus the extra duty.

Canada "Import banned": Proclamation 11061 bans 38 of the lines only when the goods are packaged in bottles, cans, boxes, kegs or similar containers for consumers; bulk goods on those lines enter at +50% (+60% without USMCA). Select a cell to see the lines.
Federal excise taxes on wine, beer and spirits (26 U.S.C. chapter 51), collected by CBP at entry, are not customs duties and are not included.

The IEEPA duties (9903.01.xx, 9903.02.xx) are still printed in the schedule but ended February 24, 2026; the Section 122 surcharge (9903.03.01) expired July 23, 2026; the aluminum duty on canned beer (9903.85.08) ended April 6, 2026. None is applied.
The rate is not the only gate: importing wine, beer or spirits for resale needs a TTB importer's basic permit and label approval (COLA), and FDA prior notice applies to every shipment.

The UK exception list (note 52(j)(1), 9903.05.96) covers all whisky of 2208.30. Note 51 lists 84 Chapter 22 lines for the Canada Section 338 duties; Proclamations 11061 and 11062 ban 81 Canadian lines (38 of them only when packaged for consumers). tariffEngineering.h1: HTS Chapter 22: Beverages, Spirits and Vinegar — Import Documents & Ways to Lower Duty

seo.title: Importing Wine, Beer & Spirits into the U.S.: TTB Permit, COLA, Excise Tax & Ways to Lower Duty (HTS Ch. 22) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: The documents and rules for each HTS Chapter 22 line — TTB importer's basic permit, certificates of label approval, excise tax at entry, wine certificates, FDA prior notice, bottled-water rules, the Canada ban — and the legal ways to pay less: USMCA and FTA claims, the UK whisky exception, Chapter 98, drawback.
keywords: how to import alcohol into the us

tariffEngineering.intro:
For alcohol the first question is **who may import it**: a business importing wine, beer or spirits for resale needs a **TTB importer's basic permit**, a **certificate of label approval (COLA)** for each label before the goods are released, and pays **federal excise tax** to CBP at entry. Wine also needs the foreign-government certificates TTB requires. Every shipment needs FDA prior notice; non-alcoholic drinks and water also fall under FDA's foreign supplier verification and bottled-water rules. Canadian alcohol is now largely banned.

The duty itself is usually small, and the ways to pay less are written into the schedule: **claim USMCA or an FTA**, check whether the **UK whisky exception** applies, use **Chapter 98** for returned U.S. goods, or claim **drawback** on re-exported product. Each depends on a document, listed below with its regulation.

levers.title: Claim USMCA on beer, tequila and other Mexican beverages
levers.saves: The base rate and the 10% Section 301 duty — $20,000 on $200,000 of Mexican beer
levers.appliesTo: All 121 lines for goods that qualify as originating under USMCA; for Canada the claim no longer removes the Section 338 duty
levers.document: A certification of origin from the importer, exporter or producer. It need not follow a prescribed format; it can be on the invoice or another document, and CBP can ask for it.
levers.caveat: For Canadian alcohol the 50% Section 338 duty applies even with a USMCA claim (U.S. note 51(a)) and most Canadian wine and spirits are banned from September 29, 2026. The USMCA was not renewed at the July 1, 2026 joint review but remains in force.

citations.label: USTR statement on the USMCA joint review (July 1, 2026)

levers.title: Claim a free trade agreement (Chile, Australia, Peru, Colombia, Korea, CAFTA-DR and others)
levers.saves: The base rate — for wine 6.3¢ to 22.4¢ per liter, for cheap rum 23.7¢ per proof liter; the Section 301 duty stays
levers.appliesTo: Lines whose Special column lists the agreement (AU, BH, CL, CO, IL, JO, KR, MA, OM, P, PA, PE, SG)
levers.document: A claim on the entry with the agreement's certification or origin information — for example Chile (19 CFR 10.410), CAFTA-DR (19 CFR 10.583) or Australia (19 CFR 10.703).
levers.caveat: An FTA claim does not remove the 2026 Section 301 duty (U.S. note 52(a)): Chilean and Australian wine still pay 12.5%.

levers.title: Enter British whisky under 2208.30 — it is on the UK exception list
levers.saves: The 10% UK Section 301 duty: $15,000 on $150,000 of Scotch
levers.appliesTo: Whisky of 2208.30 (Scotch, Irish and other) that is a product of the United Kingdom
levers.document: The normal entry under 2208.30 with the UK exception heading (9903.05.96); Scotch must meet the distinctive-product standard and TTB certificate rules.
levers.caveat: Only whisky is on the UK list: British gin, vodka, liqueurs and beer pay 10%. Irish whiskey made in Ireland is an EU product and pays the EU 10%.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 52(j)(1)

levers.title: Check the value brackets for rum, brandy and vodka
levers.saves: Rum valued over $3 per proof liter (bottled) or 69¢ (bulk) is Free instead of 23.7¢ per proof liter
levers.appliesTo: Rum (2208.40) and the brandy and vodka lines split by value per liter
levers.document: An invoice that supports the transaction value per liter or proof liter.
levers.caveat: The bracket follows the real transaction value; under-valuing to change bracket is a customs violation.

levers.title: Use a Chapter 98 provision when the facts fit
levers.saves: The base rate and the Section 301 duty: the provision below is Free
levers.appliesTo: U.S. wine, beer or spirits that were exported and come back unchanged (for example a rejected export shipment), and small trade samples of foreign alcohol
levers.document: Proof that the goods are U.S. products returned unchanged, or that the samples meet the size limits and are only for soliciting orders; TTB rules also apply.
levers.caveat: The 2026 Section 301 duties do not apply to goods properly entered under a Chapter 98 provision when CBP agrees the entry is appropriate, except 9802.00.40–9802.00.80 entries (U.S. note 52(a)).

provisions.text: Products of the United States returned after export without being advanced in value or improved in condition abroad
Alcoholic beverage samples (up to 300 ml of beer, 150 ml of wine or 100 ml of other alcoholic beverages each) used only to solicit orders by importers of commercial quantities

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 52(a)

levers.title: Claim drawback when imported beverages are exported again
levers.saves: Up to 99% of the duties paid on goods that are exported or used to make exported products
levers.appliesTo: Any line, when the imported product (or substitutable product under the same 8-digit subheading) is exported — for example bulk spirits blended and exported
levers.document: A drawback claim with import and export records linking the two.
levers.caveat: Not every extra duty is eligible for drawback, and excise-tax refunds follow separate TTB and CBP rules; confirm before pricing on it.

levers.title: Get a binding ruling before you import
levers.saves: Certainty: a ruling fixes the classification (wine vs. flavored wine, beer vs. fermented beverage, spirit type, container size) before the goods arrive
levers.appliesTo: Any line where the classification decides the rate, the ban status for Canada, or the UK exception
levers.document: A ruling request to CBP describing the product and the intended entry.
levers.caveat: Rulings apply to the transaction described; a different product may need its own.

rules.title: Importer's basic permit under the Federal Alcohol Administration Act to import wine, beer or spirits for resale
Certificate of label approval (COLA) for each label before release from customs custody
Federal excise tax on imported wine, beer and spirits, collected by CBP at entry
Foreign-government certificates of origin and of the wine's standards required for imported wine
Government health warning statement on beverages of 0.5% alcohol or more
Prior notice before arrival and food facility registration of the foreign producer
Foreign supplier verification program for non-alcoholic drinks, water and vinegar (alcoholic beverages from TTB-type facilities are exempt)
Bottled water: quality standard, labeling and processing rules
Country-of-origin marking on each bottle or can
Canadian alcohol: report 9903.03.12–9903.03.14 on listed lines; banned lines may not be entered from September 29, 2026

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 51

groups.label: Mineral water and other water (unsweetened)
groups.note: Water is an FDA food: bottled water must meet the 21 CFR 165.110 standard.

groups.label: Soft drinks and other non-alcoholic beverages
groups.note: Non-alcoholic beer of Canada is banned from September 29, 2026 (Proclamation 11062); other soft drinks are ordinary FDA foods.

groups.label: Beer made from malt
groups.note: Canadian beer in cans, bottles or kegs is banned from September 29, 2026; bulk beer pays +50%.

groups.label: Wine of fresh grapes
groups.note: Still Canadian wine up to 10 liters (including ice wine) is banned; wine needs foreign-government certificates for TTB.

groups.label: Vermouth and flavored wine
groups.note: Canadian vermouth up to 2 liters is banned from September 29, 2026.

groups.label: Cider, sake and other fermented beverages
groups.note: Hard cider, sake and hard seltzer follow the wine or malt-beverage rules depending on the product; Canadian packaged cider is banned.

groups.label: Ethyl alcohol and fuel ethanol
groups.note: Beverage alcohol needs a TTB permit; fuel and industrial ethanol follow TTB industrial-alcohol rules instead.

groups.label: Spirits and liqueurs
groups.note: Bottled Canadian whisky, vodka, rum, brandy and liqueurs are banned; UK whisky is on the Section 301 exception list.

groups.label: Vinegar
groups.note: Vinegar is an ordinary FDA food; balsamic vinegar may contain sulfites that must be declared.

finalConclusion.intro: Straight answers to the most common questions about importing wine, beer and spirits into the U.S. — tariffs by country, the Canadian ban, HS codes and the permits you need. Each answer links to the page with the full detail.
keyTakeaways: Base rates on beverages are small: beer and almost all spirits are Free, still wine 6.3¢–22.4¢ per liter, sparkling wine 19.8¢ per liter. The extra duties decide the cost.

Since July 24, 2026: EU wine, beer and spirits pay 10% in total, Japanese 12.5%, New Zealand, Australia and Chile +12.5%, the UK +10% with Scotch and Irish whisky exempt. USMCA-qualifying Mexican beer and tequila are free.

Canadian alcohol pays 50% under Section 338 even with USMCA, and from September 29, 2026 bottled Canadian wine and spirits and packaged beer and cider are banned. Importing alcohol for resale also needs a TTB permit and label approval, and excise tax is due at entry.

faqs.question: What is the U.S. tariff on imported wine right now?
faqs.answer: The base rate on still wine in bottles is 6.3¢ per liter (16.9¢ for wine over 14% such as sherry), sparkling wine 19.8¢ per liter. On top, wine from the 60 Section 301 economies pays an extra duty since July 24, 2026: EU wine 10% of value in total, New Zealand, Australia and Chile +12.5%, Argentina and the UK +10%. Most Canadian wine is banned from September 29, 2026. Federal excise tax is collected separately at entry.

faqs.question: What is the tariff on French, Italian and other European wine?
faqs.answer: EU wine pays 10% of value in total since July 24, 2026 (Section 301, 9903.05.39), because its base rate is under 10%: $7,200 on a $72,000 container of Bordeaux, the same for Champagne, Prosecco and Rioja. From August 7, 2025 to February 24, 2026 EU wine paid 15% in total under the IEEPA reciprocal tariff, which has ended. France ($2.46B) and Italy ($2.15B) were the largest wine suppliers in 2025.

faqs.question: Is there a tariff on Scotch whisky?
faqs.answer: No duty on Scotch from the UK: whisky is Free and all whisky of 2208.30 is on the United Kingdom's exception list for the 2026 Section 301 duty (U.S. note 52(j)(1), 9903.05.96). British gin, vodka and beer pay 10%. Irish whiskey made in the Republic of Ireland is an EU product and pays the EU 10%. From April 5, 2025 to February 24, 2026 Scotch paid the 10% reciprocal duty.

faqs.question: Are there tariffs on tequila and Mexican beer?
faqs.answer: Not if they qualify for USMCA, which tequila and Mexican-brewed beer normally do: both have a Free base rate, and USMCA goods are exempt from the 10% Section 301 duty on Mexico (9903.05.94). Without a valid USMCA claim they pay 10% of value. Canned beer paid the Section 232 duty on the value of its aluminum from April 4, 2025 until April 6, 2026. Mexico supplied $6.10B of beer and $3.80B of spirits in 2025.

faqs.question: Why is Canadian alcohol banned, and what is still allowed?
faqs.answer: Because Canadian provinces stopped buying and selling U.S. alcohol in March 2025, the U.S. put a 50% Section 338 duty on Canadian alcohol from August 22, 2026 and, under Proclamation 11061, banned imports from September 29, 2026: still wine up to 10 liters, ice wine, vermouth, bottled whisky, vodka, rum, brandy and liqueurs outright, and beer, cider, sparkling wine and gin when packaged for consumers. Bulk shipments of those packaged-only lines can still enter at +50% (60% without USMCA). Canadian water, soft drinks and fuel ethanol are not affected.

faqs.question: What is the tariff on Japanese whisky and sake?
faqs.answer: Japanese goods with a base rate under 12.5% pay 12.5% in total since July 24, 2026 (9903.05.49). Whisky (Free) and sake (3¢ per liter) therefore pay 12.5% of value: $12,500 on $100,000 of whisky.

faqs.question: What is the tariff on New Zealand and Australian wine?
faqs.answer: Both pay 12.5% under the 2026 Section 301 action. New Zealand wine also pays the 6.3¢/liter base rate — about 13.5% in total on $6-a-liter wine. Australian (and Chilean) wine is Free of the base rate with an FTA claim but still pays the 12.5%, which an FTA claim does not remove.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for wine?
faqs.answer: Wine of fresh grapes is heading 2204: sparkling wine and Champagne 2204.10; still wine in containers of 2 liters or less 2204.21 (red 2204.21.50.05, white .15, by alcohol and organic status); 2–10 liters (bag-in-box) 2204.22; bulk over 10 liters 2204.29. Vermouth is 2205, cider and sake 2206.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for whisky, vodka and tequila?
faqs.answer: Spirits are heading 2208: brandy and Cognac 2208.20, whisky 2208.30 (Scotch and Irish 2208.30.30, bourbon and other 2208.30.60), rum 2208.40, gin 2208.50, vodka 2208.60, liqueurs 2208.70, and tequila (2208.90.50), mezcal (2208.90.72) and other spirits under 2208.90. Almost all are Free; cheap rum and premixed cocktails pay per proof liter.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for beer?
searchedAs: hs code for non alcoholic beer
faqs.answer: Beer made from malt is 2203.00.00 (glass bottles .30, cans and other small containers .60, kegs and bulk over 4 liters .90), Free. Non-alcoholic beer (0.5% or less) is 2202.91 at 0.2¢ per liter; hard cider and hard seltzer are in 2206.

faqs.question: How do I import alcohol into the U.S. for resale?
searchedAs: how to import alcohol into the us
faqs.answer: You need a TTB importer's basic permit (27 CFR 1.20) and a certificate of label approval for each label before CBP releases the goods (27 CFR 4.40 wine, 5.24 spirits, 7.24 beer). CBP collects federal excise tax at entry (27 CFR 27.48), imported wine needs the foreign-government certificates TTB requires (27 CFR 27.140), and every shipment needs FDA prior notice (21 CFR 1.281). State licensing and the three-tier system apply after import.

faqs.question: Where does the U.S. import its beer, wine and spirits from?
faqs.answer: $28.00B of Chapter 22 goods in 2025, down 14.1%: Mexico $11.12B (beer and tequila), France $4.31B (wine and Cognac), Italy $3.34B (wine), Canada $1.56B, the UK $1.46B (Scotch), the Netherlands $942M (beer) and Ireland $608M. Beer was $7.21B, wine $6.54B and spirits $8.96B, down 26%.
